Simon looked away. His hair still had that sea smell. Esther resisted the urge to ask about salt and sun and where he slept under which stars. The drive's seal had broken before any of those questions would matter.

"The data," he said, "was copied."

She raised an eyebrow. "You mean they took the original and left a clone?"

He nodded. "I wanted to confirm."

"By breaking the seal? Without consulting me?" Esther circled around him, keeping his gaze. "What if they had made two copies?"

"Then we still have one."

Esther let out a slow breath. "You said the drive was undamaged when you recovered it."

"It was. Physically intact."

"What did you find on your copy?"

"No evidence of cloning software. Just the original files." Simon touched the damaged seal again. "But I wanted to be sure."

Esther sat on the edge of the bed and crossed her arms. "How much time did we lose verifying that your method was safe?"

"Two days."

She closed her eyes for a moment. When she opened them, she traced the outline of his collarbone with her fingertip. "You spent forty-eight hours alone making this decision."

"I know."

"Do you?"

Simon's hands clenched at his sides. His breath changed. Esther watched as he opened himself to the consequences of his choice.

When she reached the fourth button, she stopped and looked directly at him.

"Still yes?"

"Then who asked you to break it?"

He looked down at their crossed hands. "I opened it myself."

The admission made the air tighten between them. Esther released his wrist and folded her arms across her chest, her face showing neither approval nor refusal.

Simon moved toward her but stopped when his left hand touched the empty tea cup. It had been cold long before his arrival. The tea stained the floor around it with a small ring, as if the drink itself could not contain itself.

The drive waited in silence, its open port exposing data that might still prove valuable. But Simon knew they were both more concerned about what Esther's father would say about this action—if he ever found out at all.

"I understand you better than you think," Esther said, finally. Her voice held neither anger nor forgiveness, just the weight of a woman who had spent the last months trying to preserve something when the rest of their world had turned to ash. "Do you want to know what I think?"

He nodded.

"I think your mother told you to open it."

Simon closed his eyes at this. He didn't like being read so easily. But she was right.

"What did you find inside?" Esther asked, her tone revealing nothing of her feelings.

"Nothing worth the risk," he admitted.

"And now?"

"Now I've seen something I cannot unsee."

Esther tilted her head slightly.

"Show me then."
